The Story of Dhanya Muni

I bow to Lord Jinendra, who teaches the supreme dharma, and I write the story of Monk Dhanya, which brings happiness to those who read or hear it.

In the eastern part of Jambudvip, in the famous capital Vaitashokpur of the Videha region, there ruled a king named Ashok, who was extremely greedy. When harvest time came and the grain was being threshed, he would have the mouths of the poor oxen tied shut. And in the kitchen, he would have the breasts of the cooking women bound so that their babies could not nurse. Truly, what sin do greedy people not commit?

One day, a disease broke out in Ashok's mouth. His entire mouth became covered with sores. Thousands of boils and ulcers appeared on his head too. He suffered greatly. He had medicine prepared for the disease. He was just about to drink it when, by fortune, a monk came that way for alms, his feet purifying the earth. By chance, this monk was suffering from the very same disease. Seeing the monk's painful condition, the king thought, "The disease that causes me such suffering — it seems this treasure of austerity is also afflicted by it." Moved by this thought, or by compassion, the king gave the medicine he was about to drink himself to the monk, along with a proper diet.

The medicine did great good. The monk's terrible disease, which had lasted twelve years, was cured in a short time. The monk became well again.

When Ashok died, through the merit of that gift of medicine, he was reborn as Dhanya — a handsome, virtuous son of King Nishthsen and Queen Nandamati of Amalkantpur. One day, Dhanya had the opportunity to hear Lord Neminath's discourse on dharma. Learning from the Lord that his lifespan was very short, he immediately renounced all attachment and became a monk.

One day, he went into the city for alms, but through the ripening of past sinful karma, he received no alms. He returned to the meditation grove empty-handed. From there, wandering and teaching dharma, he came to Sauripur on the banks of the Yamuna and began meditating in the atapan posture. At that time, the local king had come hunting but found no game. As he was returning to his palace, his eye fell on the monk. The sinful king thought, "This naked ascetic must be the reason I found no game — he has brought me bad luck." With this thought, he ordered his men to harm the monk.

But Dhanya Muni remained unmoved, absorbed in meditation. He endured all the suffering with perfect equanimity. Seeing the monk's unwavering peace, the king's heart was transformed. He realised his mistake and bowed to the monk, asking forgiveness.

Through dedicated spiritual practice, Dhanya Muni destroyed his karmas and ultimately attained liberation.

This story teaches that compassion is a supreme virtue. King Ashok's act of giving his medicine to the suffering monk — despite his own greed and cruelty — earned him the merit to be reborn as a virtuous prince and ultimately attain liberation. And Dhanya Muni's ability to endure suffering with equanimity shows the power of spiritual practice. The wise should cultivate compassion for all beings and endure hardships with patience.
